rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).

rows.question: Does the obligation to indicate that deep-fakes are artificially generated apply when prosecuting a criminal offence?

rows.question: When the intended use of an AI system is listed in Annex III of the EU AI Act, the AI system is automatically high-risk, isn't it? If not, can you explain when that is not the case?
rows.answer: Not always. Under Article 6(2) an AI system falling within one of the lettered use cases listed under the eight areas of Annex III is high-risk, but Article 6(3) provides a derogation: such a system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and it is intended to perform a narrow procedural task, to improve the result of a previously completed human activity, to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review, or to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. That derogation never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk. A provider relying on Article 6(3) must document that assessment before placing the system on the market and still register the system in the EU database under Article 49.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No, the AI system is high-risk, because the Act recognises no "medium risk" tier and does not import the sectoral risk class of the host product. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where both conditions are met: it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes the Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment for its placing on the market. Both limbs are satisfied here, so the medical device's own "medium-risk" classification is irrelevant to the AI classification. The consequence is that the Chapter III Section 2 requirements apply to the AI system and, under Article 43(3), they are assessed as part of the MDR notified-body conformity assessment procedure, a single integrated procedure covering both regimes.

rows.question: Does the EU AI Act apply to AI systems or AI models or both?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: Not prohibited, and not high-risk on the biometrics route. Biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be is expressly excluded from the remote biometric identification use case in Annex III(1)(a), so Article 6(2) does not classify it as high-risk on that basis, and it is none of the practices banned by Article 5, which reaches biometric categorisation only where the system deduces or infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. It would nonetheless become high-risk if the verification function serves another listed Annex III use case, for example verifying candidates in recruitment or worker management under Annex III(4), or if under Article 6(1) it is a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment. Absent those conditions the system is limited risk at most, since Article 50 imposes transparency duties only on the specified interaction, synthetic-content, emotion recognition and biometric categorisation scenarios, none of which a pure identity-confirmation check engages.

rows.question: Are AI safety components within medical devices of MDR class IIa, IIb, or III considered to be high-risk according to the EU AI Act? Why?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a medical device is high-risk under Article 6(1), because both cumulative conditions are met: the product is covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR) at point 11, and a device of MDR class IIa, IIb or III must undergo a third-party conformity assessment involving a notified body before being placed on the market or put into service. Class I devices, which self-certify without notified-body involvement, do not satisfy the Article 6(1)(b) condition and are therefore not high-risk on this route. The applicable conformity assessment for such a safety component is governed by Article 43, carried out within the notified-body procedure under the MDR itself, so the Chapter III Section 2 requirements are verified through the sectoral assessment rather than a separate parallel procedure.

rows.question: What is the meaning and purpose of 'testing data' in the context of AI systems, and why is it important that it is not leaked during the training process?
rows.answer: Testing data is defined in Article 3(32) as data used to provide an independent evaluation of the AI system, in order to confirm its expected performance before it is placed on the market or put into service. If testing data leaks into the training process, the system is in effect assessed on data it has already seen, which inflates its apparent performance and defeats the purpose of the independent check that Article 10 requires for the datasets of a high-risk AI system.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.

rows.question: Which AI systems used in education or vocational training should be classified as high-risk according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Four use cases under the education and vocational training area of Annex III are high-risk, and they are classified as such by Article 6(2), which makes any AI system listed in Annex III high-risk. They are systems intended to determine access or admission or to assign natural persons to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels, systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes, including where those outcomes are used to steer the learning process, systems intended to assess the appropriate level of education that an individual will receive or be able to access, and systems intended for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests. Each applies in the context of or within educational and vocational training institutions at all levels. Under the Article 6(3) derogation such a system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, but it remains high-risk whenever it profiles natural persons, and the provider must document that self-assessment before placing the system on the market.

rows.question: What obligations, if any, does the EU AI Act set in place for AI systems that interact directly with natural persons? What exceptions, if any, apply?
rows.answer: Providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that the persons concerned are informed they are interacting with an AI system, under the transparency obligation in Article 50(1), unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and context of use. That information must be given to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, and must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements under Article 50(5). One exception applies: the disclosure duty does not attach to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties. That exception is itself reversed where such systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence, in which case the Article 50(1) disclosure is required.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibition of AI practices attracts administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, where the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, under Article 99(3). This is the highest of the three ceilings in the penalty regime, above the EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % tier in Article 99(4) for operator and notified-body breaches and the EUR 7 500 000 or 1 % tier in Article 99(5) for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or competent authorities. For SMEs, including start-ups, Article 99(6) reverses the rule so the applicable ceiling is the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount. Article 5 is the provision breached, prohibiting eight practices including subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement.

rows.question: How does Annex II relate to prohibited uses of AI systems?
rows.answer: Annex II does not itself prohibit anything. It operates as the closed list of serious criminal offences referred to in Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point (h)(iii), which is one of the three narrow exceptions to the Article 5 prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, and the offence must be punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence of at least four years. The listed offences are terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children and child pornography, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives, murder, grievous bodily injury, illicit trade in human organs or tissue, illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials, kidnapping, illegal restraint or hostage-taking, crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships, rape, environmental crime, organised or armed robbery, sabotage, and participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more of those offences. Outside those exhaustively listed offences and the other two objectives in Article 5, namely the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation and for missing persons, and the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety or a genuine and foreseeable terrorist attack, the practice remains a prohibited practice. Annex II therefore has no bearing on the other prohibitions in Article 5, such as social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images, or emotion recognition in workplaces and education institutions.

rows.question: Can the European Commission amend Annex III of the EU AI Act to add or modify use-cases classified as high-risk AI systems? Under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes, the Commission may amend Annex III by adding or modifying use-cases of high-risk AI systems through delegated acts adopted in accordance with Article 97, under Article 7(1). Both conditions must be fulfilled cumulatively: the AI systems are intended to be used in one of the areas already listed in Annex III, and they pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to or greater than the risk posed by the high-risk AI systems already referred to in Annex III. When assessing that second condition the Commission must weigh the Article 7(2) criteria, including the intended purpose, the extent of use, the nature and amount of data processed, the degree of autonomy, the severity and reversibility of harm, and the availability of redress. The Commission cannot create a new area, only add or modify use-cases within the existing areas, and Article 7(3) separately allows removal of a use-case where it no longer poses significant risks to fundamental rights, health or safety and the deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection under Union law. Procedurally, Article 97 confers the power for five years from 1 August 2024 with tacit extension, requires consultation of experts designated by each Member State before adoption, and the act enters into force only if neither the European Parliament nor the Council objects within three months of notification, extendable by a further three months.

rows.question: Should market surveilance authorities be provided with remote access to documentations and data sets used to develop a high-risk AI system?
rows.answer: Yes, where relevant and limited to what is necessary for their tasks. rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems have no mandatory duties under the Act, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.

rows.question: Does "systemic risk" apply to AI systems or general purpose AI models or both?
rows.answer: Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a model with systemic risk where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; under Article 51(2) a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations. The Commission may also designate a model on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria. A model classified as having systemic risk then carries the additional Article 55 obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, serious-incident reporting, and adequate cybersecurity. The high-risk regime for AI systems under Articles 6 and Annex III is a separate classification and does not use the systemic-risk concept.

rows.question: Are AI systems that fall under one of the areas of Annex III, but not falling within a use-case within such areas, considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Article 6(2) classifies a system as high-risk only where it falls within one of the use-cases specifically listed under the eight areas of Annex III, so a numbered area heading such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, or administration of justice and democratic processes is not itself an operative trigger. A system merely operating in such a sector, without matching a lettered use-case entry, is not high-risk on the Annex III route. It may still be high-risk on the separate Annex I route under Article 6(1), where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

rows.question: If I have an AI system that is high-risk because listed in the use cases of Annex III, and change it to a different use case that is not in Annex I or III, does it stay high-risk due to its historical provenance?
rows.answer: No, high-risk status does not attach as a matter of historical provenance. Classification under Article 6 is assessed against the system's intended purpose at the relevant time, so a system is high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I that must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation (Article 6(1)), or where it falls within one of the lettered use cases under the eight areas of Annex III (Article 6(2)). Once the intended purpose is genuinely changed to a use case listed in neither Annex I nor Annex III, and the system is no longer intended for the former Annex III use case, it is not high-risk going forward. The reclassification must be reflected in the intended purpose as declared and in the instructions for use, and it does not retroactively cure any non-compliance during the period the system was placed on the market or put into service for the Annex III use case.

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Article 1(1) states that the purpose of the Regulation is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation. rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: Unlimited jurisdiction to review. rows.question: Consider the situation in which a market surveillance authority (MSA) determines that an AI system, originally classified as non-high-risk by the provider, is in fact high-risk. Does the provider need to recall and suspend the use of the system without undue delay, or does the MSA provide a timeframe within which the provider can take corrective actions? Or does this depend on the gravity of the situation?
rows.answer: The market surveillance authority prescribes the timeframe, and immediate recall is not automatically required. Under Article 80(2), where the authority's evaluation finds that a system the provider classified as non-high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation is in fact high-risk, it must without undue delay require that provider to take all necessary actions to bring the system into compliance with this Regulation and to take appropriate corrective action within a period the authority may prescribe. The gravity of the situation does matter, because where the system also presents a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, Article 79(2) requires the authority to order corrective action, withdrawal from the market or recall within a period it may prescribe, and in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period laid down in the relevant Union harmonisation legislation. Independently of any order, Article 20 obliges the provider, once it considers or has reason to consider the high-risk AI system non-conforming, to immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring it into conformity, withdraw it, disable it or recall it, and to inform the distributors, the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers accordingly.

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.

rows.question:

rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 26(7), that information must be provided, where applicable, in accordance with the rules and procedures laid down in Union and national law and practice on the information of workers and their representatives.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict, documented access controls to prevent misuse (c); no transmission or transfer to other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what specific information must a provider/prospective provider submit (and keep up to date) regarding testing of a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside an AI regulatory sandbox?
rows.answer: The provider or prospective provider must draw up a real world testing plan and submit it to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where the testing is to be conducted, and the testing may proceed only in accordance with that approved plan under Article 60. Article 60 further requires the testing in real world conditions, and the provider or prospective provider conducting it, to be registered in the dedicated section of the EU database, which yields a Union-wide unique single identification number and the information accompanying that registration. That registered information must be kept up to date for the duration of the testing, including any suspension or termination and the outcome of the testing. Article 60 also conditions the testing on the informed consent of the test subjects and on supervision by the market surveillance authority, and the Commission specifies the detailed elements of the real world testing plan by implementing acts.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, if a deployer has reason to believe that the use of a high-risk AI system may present a risk, what must the deployer do, and whom must the deployer inform?
rows.answer: The deployer must, without undue delay, inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and must suspend the use of that system, under Article 26(5), which applies where the deployer has reason to consider that use in accordance with the instructions for use may result in the system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), namely a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights. That same paragraph requires the deployer to monitor the operation of the high-risk AI system on the basis of the instructions for use and, where relevant, to inform the provider in accordance with Article 72 on post-market monitoring. Where the deployer has identified a serious incident, it must immediately inform first the provider, and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities. If the provider cannot be reached, Article 73 on serious incident reporting applies mutatis mutandis, and the notification duty does not extend to sensitive operational data of deployers that are law enforcement authorities.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Article 13 requires a high-risk AI system to be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, and Article 13(3) prescribes the minimum content of the accompanying instructions for use. That content comprises the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance including the intended purpose, the level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, any known or foreseeable circumstance related to use in accordance with the intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse which may lead to risks to health and safety or fundamental rights referred to in Article 9(2), the system's performance as regards the persons or groups on which it is intended to be used, specifications for the input data, information enabling deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately, the changes to the system and its performance pre-determined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment, the human oversight measures referred to in Article 14 including the technical measures put in place to facilitate interpretation of outputs, the computational and hardware resources needed together with the expected lifetime and the necessary maintenance and care measures including software updates, and, where relevant, a description of the mechanisms within the system allowing deployers to properly collect, store and interpret the logs in accordance with Article 12. This information must be provided in a concise, complete, correct and clear form that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what actions must a provider take when it considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation?
rows.answer: The provider must immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring the system into conformity, to withdraw it, to disable it, or to recall it, as appropriate, under Article 20.1. It must inform the distributors of the high-risk AI system concerned and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers. Where that system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79.1 and the provider becomes aware of the risk, Article 20.2 requires it to immediately investigate the causes in collaboration with the reporting deployer, and to inform the market surveillance authorities competent for the system and, where applicable, the notified body that issued a certificate for it, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken. Article 16 anchors these duties in the provider's core obligations, requiring it to take the necessary corrective actions and provide the information required by Article 20.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, what is the definition of (a) a "conformity assessment body" and (b) "conformity assessment"?
rows.answer: A "conformity assessment body" is defined in Article 3(21) as a body that performs third-party conformity assessment activities, including testing, certification and inspection. "Conformity assessment" is defined in Article 3(20) as the process of demonstrating whether the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 relating to a high-risk AI system have been fulfilled.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Codes of conduct may be drawn up under Article 95(3) by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both, including with the involvement of any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, such as civil society organisations and academia. The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate their drawing up under Article 95(1), including the related governance mechanisms, to foster voluntary application to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems of some or all of the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2, taking account of available technical solutions and industry best practices. Under Article 95(4) the AI Office and the Member States must take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups, when doing so. A single code may cover one or more AI systems, taking into account the similarity of their intended purpose.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which AI systems in the financial services area are classified as high-risk under Annex III(5)(b), and what explicit exceptions are listed?
rows.answer: AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or to establish their credit score are high-risk under Annex III(5)(b), which sits within the Annex III area on access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits, and is classified high-risk through the Annex III use-case route in Article 6(2). The single explicit exception stated in that point is for AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud, which therefore falls outside Annex III(5)(b). Separately, insurance-related pricing is addressed in its own point, Annex III(5)(c), covering AI systems used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider established outside the EU do in order to place a high-risk AI system on the Union market?
rows.answer: A provider established in a third country must, by written mandate, appoint an authorised representative established in the Union before making its high-risk AI system available on the Union market (Article 22(1)). The provider must enable that authorised representative to perform the tasks specified in the mandate (Article 22(2)). The mandate is not merely formal: the authorised representative must terminate it, and immediately inform the relevant market surveillance authority and, where applicable, the notified body, if it has reason to consider the provider to be acting contrary to its obligations under the Regulation (Article 22(4)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Article 17(1) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to put in place a quality management system that ensures compliance with the Regulation, documented in a systematic and orderly manner in written policies, procedures and instructions. Its minimum elements are a strategy for regulatory compliance including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for the management of modifications, techniques and procedures for design, design control and design verification, techniques and procedures for development, quality control and quality assurance, examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development and their frequency, technical specifications including standards to be applied, systems and procedures for data management covering acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation and retention, the risk management system required by Article 9, the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system under Article 72, procedures for the reporting of a serious incident under Article 73, the handling of communication with national competent authorities, other relevant authorities, notified bodies and other operators, systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information, resource management including security-of-supply measures, and an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of management and other staff. Under Article 17(2) implementation of those aspects must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation, while respecting in any event the degree of rigour and level of protection needed for compliance. Providers already subject to quality management obligations or an equivalent function under sectoral Union law may include these aspects in that system under Article 17(3), and under Article 17(4) financial institutions complying with internal governance arrangements or processes under Union financial services law are deemed to fulfil the obligation, with the exception of points (g), (h) and (i).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what additional obligations apply to providers of a general-purpose AI model that is classified as a model with systemic risk?
rows.answer: Providers of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk must comply with four obligations under Article 55 in addition to the baseline Article 53 duties, namely performing model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks, assessing and mitigating possible systemic risks at Union level including their sources arising from development, placing on the market or use of the model, keeping track of, documenting and reporting without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures, and ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and for its physical infrastructure. Classification as a model with systemic risk follows Article 51, either through high-impact capabilities, presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating point operations, or by Commission decision on the Annex XIII criteria. The Article 53 baseline continues to apply, meaning technical documentation of the model per Annex XI, information and documentation for downstream providers per Annex XII, a policy to comply with Union copyright law, and a publicly available sufficiently detailed summary of the training content, and the Article 53(2) exemption for free and open-source models from the documentation duties does not extend to models with systemic risk. Compliance may be demonstrated through the codes of practice facilitated by the AI Office under Article 56 until a harmonised standard is published.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what are the four grounds on which non-compliance with the Act may be alleged (as listed in Article 79(6))?
rows.answer: Article 79.6 requires the notifying market surveillance authority to indicate whether the alleged non-compliance is due to one or more of four grounds: non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5, a failure of a high-risk AI system to meet the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, shortcomings in the harmonised standards or common specifications referred to in Articles 40 and 41 conferring a presumption of conformity, and non-compliance with Article 50. rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Three exhaustive objectives only, and each use must be strictly necessary. Article 5(1)(h) permits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes solely for the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation as well as the search for missing persons, the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons or of a genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack, and the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence for the purpose of conducting a criminal investigation, prosecution or executing a criminal penalty. That third objective is confined to the offences listed in Annex II, which enumerates terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs, weapons or nuclear material, murder, kidnapping, rape, armed robbery, organised crime, participation in a criminal organisation and environmental crime, and only where the offence is punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence of at least four years. Any such deployment further requires prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation, with an urgency exception allowing use to begin before authorisation provided it is requested without undue delay and within 24 hours, failing which use must stop immediately, and the deployer must notify the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority.

rows.question: Under Article 32 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, when is a conformity assessment body presumed to comply with the requirements in Article 31?
rows.answer: A conformity assessment body is presumed to comply with Article 31 where it demonstrates its conformity with the criteria laid down in the relevant harmonised standards, or parts thereof, the references of which have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union, and that presumption extends only in so far as those applicable harmonised standards cover those requirements (Article 32). rows.question: Who is entitled to lodge a complaint about an infringement, and to which authority must the complaint be submitted?

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure under Article 50(2) that the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. That technical solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as is technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of the various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. The marking duty does not apply to the extent the AI system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof, nor where the system is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Where information is owed to natural persons, Article 50(5) requires it to be given in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, and to conform to the applicable accessibility requirements.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what is the scientific panel of independent experts, what are its main support/advisory tasks, and what key characteristics/selection requirements apply to its members?
rows.answer: The scientific panel is a body of independent experts established by Commission implementing act under Article 68(1), adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 98(2), and intended to support the enforcement activities under the Regulation. Its main support and advisory tasks centre on Chapter V general-purpose AI models: alerting the AI Office to systemic risks, contributing to the development of tools and methodologies for evaluating the capabilities of general-purpose AI models, and advising on the classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk. That alert function operates through the qualified alert to the AI Office under Article 90(1), where the panel has reason to suspect that a general-purpose AI model poses a concrete identifiable risk at Union level. As to members, Article 68(4) requires the experts to perform their tasks with impartiality and objectivity, to ensure the confidentiality of information and data obtained, and to neither seek nor take instructions from anyone in exercising those tasks, with each expert drawing up a publicly available declaration of interests and the AI Office establishing systems and procedures to actively manage and prevent potential conflicts of interest. The implementing act must also set the conditions, procedures and detailed arrangements for the panel and its members to issue alerts and to request the assistance of the AI Office, per Article 68(5).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, if a provider identifies a serious incident during testing in real-world conditions of a high-risk AI system, what three actions must the provider take?
rows.answer: The provider must first report the serious incident to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where the incident occurred under Article 73(1), within the tiered deadlines that run from awareness (immediately and no later than 2 days for a widespread infringement or serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure, no later than 10 days where a death is involved, and no later than 15 days for other serious incidents). Second, under Article 73(6) the provider must without delay perform the necessary investigations in relation to the serious incident and the AI system concerned, including a risk assessment of the incident and corrective action. Third, the provider must cooperate with the competent authorities and, where relevant, the notified body concerned during those investigations, and must not perform any investigation involving alteration of the AI system in a way that may affect a subsequent evaluation of the causes of the incident before informing the competent authorities of such action. These duties operate alongside the conditions governing testing in real world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes under Article 60, which subjects such testing to an approved real-world testing plan and to market surveillance authority oversight.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, the obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models, taking into account the procedural guarantees under Article 94, and it entrusts the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office under Article 88(1). That allocation is without prejudice to the Commission's powers of organisation and the division of competences between the Member States and the Union under the Treaties. Under Article 88(2), market surveillance authorities may request the Commission to exercise those powers where necessary and proportionate to assist with their own tasks under the Regulation.

rows.question: What must a distributor do if it considers a high-risk AI system is not in conformity with the Act's requirements? Additionally, what extra steps are required if the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1)?

Where the high-risk AI system additionally presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), Article 24(2) requires the distributor to inform the provider or the importer of the system, as applicable, to that effect. rows.question: What are the three maximum administrative fine tiers for (a) prohibited AI practices, (b) non-compliance with obligations for high-risk AI systems and general-purpose AI (GPAI) models, and (c) supplying incorrect/incomplete/misleading information? For each tier, give the maximum amount in EUR and the alternative maximum as a percentage of worldwide annual turnover.
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibited practices carries administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, under Article 99(3). Article 99(4) sets the second ceiling at up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 %, whichever is higher, for breaches of the closed list of operator and notified-body duties: provider obligations under Article 16, authorised representative obligations under Article 22, importer obligations under Article 23, distributor obligations under Article 24, deployer obligations under Article 26, notified-body requirements under Article 31, Article 33(1), (3) and (4) or Article 34, and the transparency obligations of providers and deployers under Article 50. Supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities in reply to a request is subject to up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1 %, whichever is higher, under Article 99(5). General-purpose AI model providers are fined separately by the Commission under Article 101, up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of annual total worldwide turnover, whichever is higher, for intentional or negligent infringement of the relevant provisions, non-compliance with an information request or supply of incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, failure to comply with a requested measure, or refusal of model access for evaluation. For SMEs, including start-ups, Article 99(6) applies the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount.

criteria.judge_remark: States EUR 35,000,000 or 7% whichever higher

criteria.criterion: High-risk/GPAI obligations (Articles 16, 22, 23, 24, 26, 31, 33(1)(3)(4), 34, 50): up to EUR 15,000,000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever higher

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what is the EU database for high-risk AI systems, what categories of information must it contain, and who is the controller of that database?
rows.answer: The EU database is a central register of high-risk AI systems set up and maintained by the Commission in collaboration with the Member States under Article 71(1), covering the Annex III high-risk AI systems registered in accordance with Articles 49 and 60 as well as systems classified by their provider as not high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation, with its data machine-readable, navigable and searchable and split between a publicly accessible part and restricted sections. Under Article 71(2) the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative enters the information listed in Sections A and B of Annex VIII, while registration of testing in real world conditions under Article 60(4) carries a Union-wide unique single identification number and the information specified in Annex IX. Article 71(5) permits personal data only in so far as necessary, including the names and contact details of the natural persons responsible for registering the system who hold legal authority to represent the provider or the deployer. The Commission is the controller of the EU database, and for the law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control systems of Annex III points 1, 6 and 7 the registration sits in a secure non-public section under Article 49(4) accessible only to the Commission and the designated national authorities.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: Article 51(1) classifies a general-purpose AI model as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk on either of two alternative conditions: it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks, or the Commission decides, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, that it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those high impact capabilities, having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII. No, the conditions are not cumulative, because Article 51(1) requires only that the model meet any of those conditions, so either route alone suffices. Article 51(2) adds a rebuttable presumption of high impact capabilities where the cumulative amount of computation used for training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than 10^25 FLOPs. Once so classified, the provider owes the Article 55 obligations, namely state-of-the-art model evaluation including documented adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, reporting of serious incidents to the AI Office without undue delay, and adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure, in addition to the Article 53 duties on technical documentation, downstream-provider information, copyright policy, and the training-content summary.

That duty applies only to the extent the deployer exercises control over the input data. rows.question: I am a distributor of an AI systems. Do I have obligation not to jeopardize its conformity? I was not told if the system is high-risk or not. What if am I am importer instead?
rows.answer: Yes, where the system is high-risk. Article 24 requires the distributor, before making a high-risk AI system available on the market, to verify that it bears the required CE marking, that it is accompanied by a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the instructions for use, and that the provider and the importer have complied with their respective obligations. Article 24 also bars the distributor from making the system available where it considers, or has reason to consider on the basis of the information in its possession, that the system does not conform with the Section 2 requirements, until conformity is restored, and it must inform the provider or the importer where the system presents a risk. Because these duties attach only to high-risk AI systems, the distributor should establish the classification with the provider before making the system available. Acting instead as an importer, the operator's duties sit in Article 23, which requires it to verify before placing the high-risk AI system on the market that the relevant conformity assessment procedure under Article 43 has been carried out.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No, not automatically. Article 6(1) makes a safety component high-risk only where both conditions are met: the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices at Annex I point 11, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment for its placing on the market under that sectoral legislation. A Class I device that is non-sterile, without a measuring function and not reusable surgical is self-certified by the manufacturer without notified body involvement, so the second condition in Article 6(1)(b) fails and the Annex I route does not classify the system as high-risk. The system could still be high-risk on the separate route in Article 6(2) if its intended purpose falls within one of the lettered use cases under the eight areas of Annex III, such as biometrics or critical infrastructure. Absent that, it is not high-risk, and any reclassification of the device to Class IIa, IIb or III, or the addition of a sterile, measuring or reusable surgical characteristic triggering notified body assessment, would bring it within Article 6(1).

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), can the same AI system be subject both to the Act's "high-risk AI system" obligations and to the transparency obligations sometimes described informally as "limited risk"? Explain briefly.
rows.answer: Yes, the two regimes apply cumulatively to the same system. The transparency obligations in Article 50 attach to a system's characteristics rather than to its risk tier, so a high-risk AI system that also exhibits one of those characteristics must satisfy both sets of duties. Concretely, the provider must design a system intended to interact directly with natural persons so that the person is informed they are interacting with an AI system (Article 50(1)) and must mark synthetic outputs in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(2)), while the deployer must inform natural persons exposed to an emotion recognition or biometric categorisation system (Article 50(3)) and disclose image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake (Article 50(4)). The deep fake disclosure does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, and where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work it is limited to disclosure in a manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a toy qualify as a high-risk AI system, and if so under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes, where both conditions of Article 6(1) are satisfied: the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a toy, or is itself a toy, covered by Directive 2009/48/EC on the safety of toys, which appears at point 2 of Annex I as Union harmonisation legislation. The second, deciding condition is that the toy must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service under that Directive. If the toy may instead be self-assessed by the manufacturer, the Article 6(1) route is not triggered and the AI system is not high-risk on that basis, irrespective of whether it is placed on the market independently of the toy. Where the classification does bite, the provider must undergo the conformity assessment under Article 43, and a new conformity assessment is required upon any substantial modification under Article 43(4), while pre-determined changes already documented at the initial assessment do not count as such., so the practical test in each case is whether Directive 2009/48/EC itself mandates notified-body involvement for that particular toy.
